name: HIV (antibody/antigen screen)
summary: A laboratory HIV antigen/antibody ("4th generation" combo) screen looks for both antibodies the immune system makes against HIV and the p24 antigen, a viral protein that appears in blood before antibodies develop.
whatItMeans: A non-reactive (negative) result means no HIV antigen or antibody was detected in the sample, though a very recent exposure can still be missed. A reactive (positive) screen is not a diagnosis on its own: it must be followed by confirmatory testing (such as an HIV-1/HIV-2 differentiation immunoassay, historically a Western blot, or a nucleic acid test) before HIV infection is confirmed. Because tests only turn reactive after seroconversion, an exposure within the window period (roughly 18-45 days for a lab antigen/antibody test) can produce a non-reactive result even when infection has occurred, so retesting is advised after a possible recent exposure.
